title: A royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9)
hookLine: every baptized person shares Christ's priesthood (CCC 1268)

cards: At a Catholic baptism, just after the water, the priest or deacon takes a small vessel of perfumed oil called chrism and anoints the crown of the baby's head. It's over in seconds, often under the sound of a crying baby.
But the prayer said over that moment is startling. It says this child is now joined to Christ, who was anointed priest, prophet and king. A priest: a newborn who can't yet hold up her own head.
The idea comes straight out of today's verse.

teach.b: Peter is writing to ordinary people: household servants, wives, converts living as strangers in their own towns.
In the Douay-Rheims: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." The phrases are borrowed.

At Mount Sinai, in the book of Exodus, God told Israel they would be a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. Peter gives those old titles to these scattered Christians, without taking them away from anyone.

A few verses earlier he says they are living stones, built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices. So what does a priest do? Stands between God and the world, and offers things up.
The Catechism puts it plainly: every baptized person shares in the priesthood of Christ, the common priesthood of the faithful.

It also teaches that the ordained priesthood is different, not just a higher level of the same thing, but a distinct gift for serving the whole people, especially at the altar. Both are real; neither replaces the other.
On a Thursday, what does that look like? Paul gives a hint in Romans: "present your bodies a living sacrifice."
The sacrifice is the day itself: the commute, the spreadsheet, the diaper, the hospital shift, the patience with a difficult relative, offered to God.

teach.h: A KINGLY PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION.
teach.b: Some Catholics begin each morning with a traditional prayer called the Morning Offering, giving God the prayers, works, joys and sufferings of the day ahead. A whole day, held up like bread at the altar.

how: Catholics are anointed with chrism at baptism as sharers in Christ's role as priest, prophet and king, and some pray a Morning Offering each day, giving God their prayers, works, joys and sufferings; the Church distinguishes this common priesthood of all the baptized from the ordained priesthood.

Exodus 19: a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.

games.q: you work a long shift at a hospital, and you're not ordained. what priestly work does Peter say is yours?
o: offering spiritual sacrifices, including the day itself.
games.why: Peter calls all the baptized a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices. the Church keeps preaching and the altar for the ordained; the offering of a life belongs to everyone.

practice: Walk through what's left of today: the work, the people, the chores, the thing you're dreading. Gather it all up in your hands, the good and the dull together, and lift it the way a priest lifts the bread at Mass.
If you pray, offer it to God, perhaps with the Morning Offering; if not, hold the day up and look at it with care.

wordCard.voice: A royal priesthood. First Peter two nine: in Catholic teaching, every baptized person shares in Christ's priesthood, offering up their life. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), the same words as the Greek of Exodus 19:6.

carryVoice: Your line: a royal priesthood. And that's week eighty-seven: angels unawares, from above, doers not hearers, faith that works, the prayer of faith, gold tested by fire, and a royal priesthood. Week eighty-seven, complete.
